analysis.one_liner: Requires safe storage of firearms and ammunition in homes where minors or prohibited people could access them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced January 4, 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it; it received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal offense to keep a gun or ammunition in a home in a way that could allow a minor to get it without permission, or to store it where a resident who is barred from owning guns could reach it. To comply, owners would have to lock the unloaded gun in a Department of Justice-certified safe with a certified trigger lock, or keep it off-site at a certified storage facility or gun range. Violations without a discharge would bring a fine of up to $5,000 in a civil action; violations that result in a discharge could bring a fine of $50,000 to $100,000, up to 20 years in prison, or both, and the court would order the Attorney General to seize and store the guns at the owner's expense.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially households where a child could get hold of an unsecured gun, and residents living with someone legally barred from owning firearms. Safely stored guns sharply reduce accidental shootings and unauthorized access by children.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with children and unsecured guns

how_it_helps.text: The bill criminalizes storing a firearm or ammunition in a residence if a minor is likely to gain access without permission or if a resident is ineligible to possess a firearm, unless the weapons are secured unloaded in a certified safe with a trigger lock or kept off-site [S2][S3].

Safe storage reduces children's access to unsecured household guns, the leading source of accidental and youth firearm deaths; the bill is named for a victim of the 2018 Santa Fe, Texas school shooting (general knowledge).

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners would bear compliance costs: a DOJ-certified safe and certified trigger lock, or paid off-site storage at a certified facility or gun range. On conviction after a discharge, the owner would also pay the government's cost to seize and store the firearms, and could face fines up to $100,000 and 20 years in prison.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners paying for certified safes or storage

drawbacks.text: Compliance is expensive and mandatory only through DOJ-certified equipment: owners must buy a certified safe and certified trigger lock or pay for off-premises storage at a certified facility or gun range, with certification standards set by the Attorney General [S3].

The penalties are steep relative to the conduct: a violation that results in a discharge carries a fine of $50,000 to $100,000, up to 20 years' imprisonment, or both, and courts must order seizure and paid storage of the firearms even for accidental discharges with no injury [S3].

The bill directs the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives to investigate every report of improper storage, which critics would view as intrusive monitoring of lawful households, and civil liberties and gun-rights groups opposed similar federal safe-storage mandates (general knowledge).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is real: unsecured household guns are a major source of child deaths, and mandated locked storage demonstrably reduces access. But the bill's design is heavy-handed: it relies entirely on a new DOJ certification regime, attaches criminal penalties including long prison terms to accidental discharges, and requires seizure and storage at the owner's expense. A narrower version tied to actual harm or focused on subsidized locks would face less objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, then sent to its Crime subcommittee in March 2021, and neither the committee nor the House ever considered it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress [S1][S5].

It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and on March 1, 2021 was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; that was the bill's last action of record [S5].
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, so it never built the support needed to move out of committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms industry avoided new mandatory storage rules and compliance costs; families with unsecured guns gained nothing, and the bill's target protections never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners; no new storage rules

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Jerry Nadler (D)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after its referral, and never reported it to the House

against.name: House Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 1, 2021 and took no recorded action on it

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats (the sponsor and two cosponsors) attached their names and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no stated opposition, though the bill sat untouched in a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Gun owners and households with firearms
industries.note: Owners in homes with minors or residents barred from gun possession would face mandatory purchase of a DOJ-certified safe and trigger lock or paid off-site storage, plus fines up to $5,000 for civil violations and far heavier criminal exposure if a violation results in a discharge. The same requirements are the mechanism protecting children in those homes.

industries.industry: Safe, trigger lock, and lockbox manufacturers
industries.note: The bill mandates that compliant storage use a DOJ-certified safe and certified trigger lock, creating a nationwide required purchase of certified equipment.

industries.industry: Gun ranges and firearms storage facilities
industries.note: Off-premises storage at a DOJ-certified facility or gun range is one of the bill's two compliance paths, opening paid storage business. Ranges already exist for the shooting sports, so the public's interest in safe storage runs alongside this new service market.

The bill does not restrict sales, but required certified-storage compliance adds a real cost to household gun ownership, which could modestly depress demand while also driving safe-and-lock accessory purchases.
